articles.title: Message Queues Explained Using a Cafe Example
articles.excerpt: What Is a Message Queue? Imagine a busy café during lunch time. Many customers place orders at Instead, the cashier writes each order on a ticket and puts it on a That ticket rack is like a message qu…
articles.body: What Is a Message Queue? Imagine a busy café during lunch time. Many customers place orders at once, but the café has only four chefs. If the cashier had to wait for a chef to finish every order before accepting the next one, the line would move very slowly. Instead, the cashier writes each order on a ticket and puts it on a rack. The chefs pick up tickets when they are ready to cook. The cashier can keep accepting orders while the chefs work through the queue. That ticket rack is like a message queue in software: it temporarily stores tasks or messages so the sender and receiver do not need to work at exactly the same time.

articles.title: Why I Made APX Stop Reading When You Take the Browser
articles.excerpt: The browser is where agent work starts to feel useful—and where a vague idea of control becomes dangerous. An agent can open a page, read it, click through a flow, and fill ordinary fields. Then a log…
articles.body: The browser is where agent work starts to feel useful—and where a vague idea of control becomes dangerous. An agent can open a page, read it, click through a flow, and fill ordinary fields. Then a login page, a 2FA challenge, or a payment form appears. At that moment I do not want a polite convention saying “the human is in charge.” I want the runtime to enforce it. That is why I made APX stop reading a tab when I take the browser wheel. A handoff is not a message to the agent. It is a control-state change that blocks agent calls. This sounds like a small implementation detail. It changed how I think about agent browser work. Watching is not the same as controlling APX V2 can give an agent an embedded browser tab. On desktop, I can see that tab while the agent works.

articles.title: Stripe webhook 401 on Supabase Edge Functions: verify_jwt is blocking it
articles.excerpt: Checkout works. Stripe's dashboard shows the webhook failing with 401. Your Edge Function logs are empty for that timestamp. That combo is almost never your Stripe code. It's the Supabase JWT check ru…
articles.body: Checkout works. Stripe's dashboard shows the webhook failing with 401 . Your Edge Function logs are empty for that timestamp. That combo is almost never your Stripe code. It's the Supabase JWT check running before your handler. What it looks like In Stripe Workbench, open the endpoint and look at a failed delivery. The response body comes from the platform, not from your return new Response(...) : { "code" : 401 , "message" : "Missing authorization header" } Sometimes it's Invalid JWT instead. Same thing. Other tells: No invocation in the function logs for that delivery. The function works when you call it yourself with Authorization: Bearer <anon key> . Local stripe listen + supabase functions serve --no-verify-jwt works, production 401s.

articles.title: Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon?
articles.excerpt: Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a collision between Earth and a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia.
articles.body: For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon , pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms. Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins , and how long has it orbited Earth? Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours .

It took them just over 27 hours to take down the Ender Dragon in what is believed to be a world first. Of course, it’s not as simple as just turning up and firing arrows at the thing. The enRage mod, created by nicklovin99, tracks how individual enemies feel about you. This works largely the same way as Shadow of War's much-loved Nemesis System, creating rivalries on the fly and disrupting the ranks of rival gangs. And, like the Nemesis System, enRage names every single NPC in the game. Some like you, some fear you, and some want you dead. It groups people by gangs, groups, and affiliations, so you’ve got the O’Driscoll Boys, Lemoyne Raiders, the U.S. Army, The Klan, the Wapiti people, the Bronte Family, the Murfee Brood, the Skinner Brothers, Van der Linde, and unaffiliated randoms. articles.title: Returning the first samples from a Martian moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission to Mars
articles.excerpt: Japan's mission to Mars' moons could answer a decades old question dividing the origins of Phobos and Deimos between two conflicting theories, and make history as the first spacecraft to return to Ear…
articles.body: Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system. The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago. articles.title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed)
articles.excerpt: The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering programmer who helped NASA land Apollo astronauts on the moon. But we will always have her example to inspire us.
articles.body: Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton , who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood. Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself. As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men?
